openings.name: Italian Game (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O O-O
openings.overview: The Italian Game is the first opening every chess player should learn — and the one most never stop playing. Documented in Pedro Damiano's 1512 chess treatise and refined by Greco's 1620s manuscripts, the Giuoco Piano ('Quiet Game') is one of the oldest analyzed openings in chess history. Paul Morphy demonstrated its devastating attacking potential in his 1858 European tour; in the modern era, Carlsen revived the slow d3 system as White's main weapon, and the c3+d4 IQP lines have become standard tournament fare. Why is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 so timeless? Because it develops two perfect pieces in two moves, points the bishop at the weakest square in chess (f7), and asks Black: 'What's your plan?' Most Black players don't have one. Levy teaches this as his foundational 1.e4 weapon because the strategic ideas are timeless. The bonus: club players almost always blunder by move 12 if they haven't studied the c3+d4 break. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: f7 is the target, full stop. Bc4 + Nf3 + Ng5 (in some lines) all aim at the f7-square. In the Italian, every tactical opportunity ultimately traces back to the bishop on c4 and the pawn on f7 defended only by the king.

The c3+d4 sequence is the engine. Play c3 to prepare d4, then push d4 to open the centre. If Black takes (exd4), you recapture cxd4 building a centre pawn duo. If Black ignores you (Nf6, O-O), you take dxe5 and grab space. Every Italian middlegame plan starts with d4.

When the isolated d-pawn appears (after Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5), DON'T sweat it. The isolated d4-pawn controls c5 and e5, gives your pieces central squares, and the Bd3 + Qd3 battery aimed at h7 wins games. The 'isolated pawn weakness' is endgame theory; you're playing the middlegame.

If Black plays the Hungarian Defence (...Be7), the Italian becomes the positional Italian. Set up d3, c3, Re1, Nbd2, then plan h3 + Nh2 + f4 for a slow kingside attack. Different style, same opening — you choose the speed.
traps: Against 3...Nf6 (Two Knights), if Black plays 4...Bc5 the Two Knights becomes a Giuoco Piano hybrid — and you can launch 5.d4! immediately. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nbxd2 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5, you reach the IQP position with full development and Black has spent two tempos on the dark-squared bishop trade.
warnings: NEVER play d4 before castling. The classic amateur disaster: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d4? exd4 5.Nxd4? Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Nf6 — Black develops with attack on the queen, then Black castles and you've spent two queen moves while Black caught up.

Count defenders of e4 every time you move the f3-knight. If you play Ng5 (attacking f7) but e4 is now undefended, Black has ...Nxe4! and the tactical adventure backfires. The e4-pawn is fragile in the Italian.

variations.name: Giuoco Piano c3-d4
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 cxd4 Bb4+ Bd2 Bxd2+ Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O O-O
variations.explanation: The Giuoco Piano's main line — 'the Quiet Game' that's anything but. After 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4! exd4 6.cxd4, Black's d4-pawn target is staring at the Bc5. The natural defence is 6...Bb4+ — but this only delays the trade. 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nbxd2 (NOT Qxd2 — the knight wants the d2-square to reroute via f1-g3) 8...d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 trades the e-pawn for Black's d-pawn, leaving White with an isolated d4-pawn. Both sides castle. This is the textbook IQP position — White has the active pieces (Nd2 heading to f1-g3, Bd3 eyeing h7, queen ready to swing), Black has the slightly better structure. Play it dynamically: every IQP middlegame is won by the side that attacks first.

variations.name: Slow Italian d3
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 O-O d6 c3 a6 a4 Ba7 Re1 O-O Nbd2 Be6
variations.explanation: When you don't want the IQP fireworks, 4.d3 is the calm system. You set up the Italian formation behind a closed centre: 5.O-O O-O 6.c3 (preparing d4 later) 6...d6 (Black mirrors) 7.a4 (preventing Black's …b5 expansion) 7...a6 — Black plays the prophylaxis dance. 8.a4 Ba7 (Black avoids the b6/a5 trade) 9.Re1 O-O 10.Nbd2 Be6 — both sides develop in mirror image. The middlegame plan: White wants Nf1-g3-Nh4 + f4 break; Black wants the same idea reversed. Same skill on both sides means a draw; better technique wins.

variations.name: Evans Gambit
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O d6 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3 Bg4
variations.explanation: Captain Evans's 1820 invention — still terrifying 200 years later. 4.b4! sacrifices a pawn to gain a tempo (4...Bxb4) and then 5.c3 chases the bishop while preparing d4. Black's best retreat is 5...Ba5 (5...Bc5 hangs to d4 with tempo; 5...Bd6 blocks the d-pawn). Now 6.d4 exd4 7.O-O d6 8.cxd4 Bb6 — you've built a massive centre AND castled in 8 moves, while Black has moved the bishop three times. Black's 9...Bg4 tries to pin the f3-knight, but you respond with 10.Bb2 + Nc3 + Qb3 piling up on the kingside. The Evans was Kasparov's surprise weapon against Anand at Riga 1995 — a 25-move kingside attack ended the game.

openings.name: London System (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 Bf4 c5 e3 Nc6 Nbd2 e6 c3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3 b6 O-O Bb7
openings.overview: Levy's signature d4 opening — the system that built an empire. The London System takes its name from the 1922 London tournament where the world's best players experimented with it; Capablanca employed it occasionally, but it remained a tournament sideline for decades until Russian masters Petrosian and Botvinnik used it for ultra-solid drawing weapons. The modern boom came when Carlsen began playing it at the elite level in the 2010s — proving that 'systems' could compete with sharp theoretical lines. The London works against literally anything Black plays: d5, Nf6, g6, c5. You set up the same pieces every game (d4, Nf3, Bf4, e3, Bd3, Nbd2, c3, O-O), learn five typical plans, and play 200 games before you ever have to think about move 6. The trade-off: against precise opponents Black equalises easily, so the London is a winning weapon at 1500 and a drawing weapon at 2200. Pick your battles. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: Bf4 BEFORE e3 — non-negotiable. If you play e3 first the dark-squared bishop is trapped behind its own pawn chain forever. The whole opening pivots on this move order.
The pyramid d4–e3–c3 is the London's structural backbone. It's nearly unbreakable from the front; Black has to find counterplay on the flanks instead of the centre, which most amateurs can't do.

Ne5 is the attacking piece. Once you've got Nf3 + Bd3 + O-O, the manoeuvre Nf3–e5 plants a knight in the heart of the position with support from f4 and Bd3 — combined with a future Qf3 or Rf3 lift, this becomes a real kingside attack.

The e4 break is the late-middlegame trick. After everyone's developed and Black thinks the position is locked, you suddenly play e3–e4 opening the centre with all your pieces aimed at the kingside — and the Bd3 finally gets to do its job.
traps: If Black tries to trade your prized Bf4 with …Nh5 hitting it, just retreat to g3 — the bishop stays useful AND now …Nh5 has wasted Black's time. Often you can follow up with Ne5 punishing the misplaced knight.
warnings: DON'T play e3 before Bf4 — the bishop is locked behind the pawn chain permanently, and at that point you're playing a worse Colle System instead of a London.
The …Qb6 / b2 weakness is the London's only structural soft spot. Always play c3 early — without it, Black's …Qb6 can win the b2-pawn or force awkward defensive moves.

variations.name: Standard Setup vs d5
variations.pgn: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 Bf4 c5 e3 Nc6 Nbd2 e6 c3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3 b6 O-O Bb7 Qe2 Bxg3 hxg3 Qc7 dxc5 bxc5 e4 h6 Rad1 Rfe8
variations.explanation: The textbook London vs Black's …d5 setup. Both sides develop sensibly; the Bxg3 trade (forced after Bd6) gives White the h-file for the rook AND opens the f-file for the queen lift. The thematic e4 break opens the centre at exactly the right moment — once Black has committed to …b6/…Bb7 and can't easily reroute pieces back. The resulting middlegame favours the side that knows the plan, which is you.

variations.name: vs King's Indian (Bh6 + Opposite-Side Castle Attack)
variations.pgn: d4 Nf6 Bf4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Qd2 O-O Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6 c5 O-O-O
variations.explanation: Levy's anti-KID weapon — NOT the quiet Be2/e3 London. Against …g6, you play sharply with Nc3 + Qd2 + Bh6! to trade off Black's fianchettoed bishop (the heart of KID defence), then castle queenside so your own kingside pawns can storm forward with h4–h5. The structural trade-off (giving up the dark-squared bishop) is worth it because Black's Bg7 was the only piece defending the king's dark squares. Source: Levy's 'London vs KID/Grünfeld Complete Guide' (YouTube/Lichess).

variations.name: Aggressive Jobava-London Hybrid
variations.pgn: d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6 e3 c5 Nf3 a6 Be2 Nc6 O-O Bd6 Bxd6 Qxd6 Na4 cxd4 exd4 O-O
variations.explanation: A more aggressive setup blending London structure with Jobava ideas — Nc3 instead of the calm Nbd2. The Na4 manoeuvre is the kicker: after the dark-bishop trade, the knight reaches a4 from where it eyes b6 and c5 — gripping the queenside dark squares. White concedes the bishop pair but gets lasting positional pressure on a half-open c-file.

openings.name: Stafford Gambit Refutation (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 Nc6 Nxc6 dxc6 d3 Bc5 Be2 h5 c3 Ng4 d4
openings.overview: The Stafford Gambit was buried in chess obscurity for nearly a century — invented by American master Joseph Stafford in the 1950s, considered unsound by every serious analyst, and forgotten. Then IM Eric Rosen turned it into a YouTube phenomenon in 2019, racking up millions of views with Stafford traps against unprepared club players. Levy made the natural follow-up: the refutation video that taught the WHITE side how to crush it. The result is that today, half the chess world plays the Stafford and the other half memorised the antidote. The correct line is the most common Stafford position you'll face: someone tried to trick you with 1…e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 (NOT 2…Nc6) hoping for 3.Nxe5 Nc6!? The fix is simple: take the pawn, then play d3 (not d4!) and just consolidate. White is up a clean pawn for nothing — Black has zero compensation against accurate play. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: d3, NEVER d4. The whole Stafford depends on Black's pieces leaping out after d4 opens central diagonals — d3 keeps the position closed and the extra pawn permanent.
Develop Be2 (not Bc4!) for fast castling. Bc4 looks active but it gets harassed by …h5+…Ng4 ideas; Be2 is bland but unprovokable.
Once you've castled, the Stafford fades to nothing. Black's whole 'attack' is one knight on g4 hitting f2 — if your king is on g1 and h3 is available, there's literally nothing for Black.
Don't get fancy. The Stafford refutation is one of the few openings where you WIN by playing the most boring move every time. Trade pieces, simplify, win the endgame.
traps: DON'T fall for 5.d4? after Nxc6 dxc6. Black plays 5…Bd6! preparing …Qe7 hitting e4 and …Ng4 hitting f2 — and the lost tempo of …d4 means White's centre collapses. Always d3 here, never d4.
warnings: Don't play d4 in the first six moves under any circumstance. The Stafford's tactical points (…Ng4, …Qh4) all depend on the f2-pawn being weak after d4 opens the centre.
When Black tries the standard Stafford bait (…h5 + …Ng4 + …Qh4), DON'T capture material. Just play h3 kicking the knight, then castle. Black has no follow-up and your extra pawn wins.

variations.name: Main Refutation d3
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 Nc6 Nxc6 dxc6 d3 Bc5 Be2 h5 c3 Ng4 d4
variations.explanation: The textbook refutation. After 4.Nxc6 dxc6, you play 5.d3 (NOT 5.d4!) keeping the centre closed and the extra pawn permanent. The Be2 development is deliberately modest — bland but unprovokable. Black's standard …h5 + …Ng4 + …Qh4 attacking battery never gets going against a calmly defended kingside. From here you just castle, trade pieces, win the endgame.

variations.name: 4...dxc6 5.e5 Line
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 Nc6 Nxc6 dxc6 e5 Ne4 d3 Nc5 Be3 Ne6 Nd2
variations.explanation: The aggressive alternative — push e5 to kick the f6-knight forward. After …Ne4, you've gained space at the cost of slightly weakening e5 itself. The follow-up plan is d3 (always d3!) attacking the knight, then Bxc5 trading off Black's most active piece. The extra pawn is intact and you've gained a strong central pawn — a slight improvement on the main refutation when you want to attack rather than consolidate.

openings.name: Caro-Kann Defense (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7
openings.overview: Named after German amateur Horatio Caro and Austrian master Marcus Kann who independently analyzed the opening in the 1880s, the Caro-Kann became respectable when Capablanca made it his preferred drawing weapon in the 1920s; Tigran Petrosian raised it to championship status in the 1960s with his impenetrable defensive treatment; Anatoly Karpov played it through his entire World Championship career. The Caro-Kann is the French Defence minus the bad bishop problem. You support d5 with c6 (instead of …e6 like the French), which means the c8-bishop escapes via f5 BEFORE you commit the e-pawn. The structure is solid as bedrock; the worst-case outcome for Black is a slightly worse endgame that requires precise technique to win. Perfect for players who hate the calculation-heavy Sicilian and Najdorf but still want serious chances with Black. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: The c6+d5 spine is the whole opening. Defend d5, develop pieces around it, never let White's e4 (or e5) push through. The pawn chain itself does half the strategic work for you.
Bf5 BEFORE e6 — this is the Caro-Kann's only real advantage over the French. Get the light-squared bishop to f5 (or g6 after harassment) before locking it in with …e6.
Knights to Nd7 and Ngf6 (in that order), NOT to c6. The d7-knight supports the …c5 and …e5 breaks AND doesn't block your own queen — a far more flexible square than c6.

Aim for the endgame. The Caro-Kann pawn structure is structurally better than White's in most middlegame trades (open lines on the queenside, no pawn islands). The slightly worse middlegame becomes a slightly better endgame with each pair of pieces traded.
traps: In the Advance Variation (3.e5), reply 3…Bf5 (developing first), then meet White's 4.Nf3 with 4…e6 and look for the …c5 break the moment White commits to a slow plan. Don't let White consolidate.
warnings: NEVER play …Bf5 after …e6. The bishop is then trapped on c8 forever and you have a worse French.

The Fantasy Variation (3.f3) is the Caro player's nightmare. It looks slow but creates a tactical mess where most Caro-Kann players (who hate calculation) get steamrolled. Be ready with concrete 3…e6 lines if it might appear.

variations.name: Classical 4...Bf5 (Main Line)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bd2 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7
variations.explanation: The Caro's headline variation — the one any 1.e4 player you face has prepared. Walk it carefully. 3...dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 — the move that separates the Caro from the French. Your bishop comes out of the chain BEFORE …e6 traps it. 5.Ng3 Bg6 (the bishop steps back to keep the diagonal). White's 6.h4 h6 7.Nf3 Nd7 8.h5 Bh7 is the classical chase — your bishop ends on h7 looking passive, but it's not actually lost a tempo because h2-h5 also cost White two pawn moves. 9.Bd3 Bxd3 10.Qxd3 trades off the light-squared bishops and centralises White's queen. Black completes development with 10...e6 11.Bd2 Ngf6, and 12.O-O-O Be7 reaches the critical position. White's queenside castling promises kingside attack with g4-g5; Black's plan is …Qa5 + …O-O-O too, OR …c5 break to open the c-file before White can mount the storm. The position is one of the most analysed in chess history — full of subtleties, but Black's position is genuinely fine.

variations.name: Classical Capablanca 4...Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.h4
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 h5 Bh7 Nf3 Nd7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7 Kb1 O-O Ne5
variations.explanation: The Capablanca version of the Classical — White invests two tempos in h4–h5 to chase Black's light-squared bishop to h7 (where it's permanently passive). The trade-off: Black's structure stays bulletproof and the h-pawns create symmetrical weaknesses you can exploit later. After Ne5 (White's typical kingside outpost), counter with …Nd7 challenging the knight and prepare the …c5 break to crack the centre.

variations.name: Tartakower / Two Knights 3...Nf6
variations.pgn: e4 c6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Nf6 e5 Ne4 Ne2 Qb6 d4 e6 Ng3 Nxg3 hxg3 c5
variations.explanation: The modern way of handling 2.Nc3 — pioneered at top level by Tartakower and revived in the engine era. By playing …Nf6 directly (skipping …dxe4), you provoke White's e5 push, then retreat the knight to e4 where it occupies a useful central square. The …Qb6 + …c5 plan hits b2 and undermines d4 simultaneously, giving Black sharper play than the classical lines.

variations.name: Two Knights 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4
variations.pgn: e4 c6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 d4 Nf6 Bd3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Nd7 O-O Nf6
variations.explanation: Levy's course recommendation when facing 2.Nc3. The …Bg4 trade is deliberate — you concede the bishop pair to eliminate White's most active piece and reach a structurally pristine position. After …Bxf3 Qxf3, White's queen is on a slightly awkward square, the centre is flexible, and Black has clear plans (…e6, …Nf6, …Be7, …O-O) with no theoretical complications. Easiest Caro line to play if you don't want to memorise the Classical.

variations.name: Advance Variation 3.e5 Bf5
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nf3 e6 Be2 c5 Be3 Nd7 O-O Ne7 Nbd2 Nc6 c3 cxd4 cxd4
variations.explanation: When White plays the Advance with 3.e5, the Caro player's superpower kicks in: Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before …e6 locks it in. This is the entire structural advantage over the French Defence. The …c5 break undermines White's d4 base; the knight route Nd7–Ne7–Nc6 is unusual but lands the knight on its best square. The resulting French-like position has Black's c8-bishop active — a permanent edge.

variations.name: Advance Variation 3.e5 c5
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 c5 dxc5 e6 a3 Bxc5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 Nge7 b4 Bb6
variations.explanation: The principled but unusual reply — instead of developing first, hit the centre immediately. After dxc5, you've handed White a queenside pawn majority, but in return you get rapid development with tempo: …Nc6 hitting c5, then …Bg4 pinning the f3-knight which defends e5. If White doesn't react precisely, …Bxf3 followed by …Nxe5 grabs back the pawn AND keeps the better position.

variations.name: Exchange Variation 3.exd5
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 Bd3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Bf4 Bg4 Qb3 Qd7 Nd2 e6 Ngf3 Bd6 Bxd6 Qxd6 O-O O-O
variations.explanation: Probably the most harmless line White has — Black recaptures …cxd5 and reaches a Carlsbad-style symmetrical structure. With the open c-file available for the …Rc8 idea (something White can't easily emulate without weakening the queenside), Black has all the long-term winning chances. Position is theoretically equal but psychologically Black is the only side trying.

variations.name: Panov-Botvinnik Attack 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 cxd5 Nxd5 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O Nc6 d5 Na5 Re1 Nxb3 axb3
variations.explanation: Levy's recommended Panov defence — the fianchetto setup with …g6 + …Bg7. White's c4 push creates the isolated d-pawn structure; you target d4 from g7 (the long diagonal) and eliminate White's most active piece (the c4-bishop) with the …Nb6–Na5 manoeuvre forcing the trade. The resulting middlegame has Black with the bishop pair plus dynamic piece play — engines call it equal but practically Black scores well.

variations.name: Fantasy Variation 3.f3
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4 e5 Nf3 Bg4 Bc4 Nd7 O-O Ngf6 c3 Bd6
variations.explanation: The Caro player's nightmare — White builds a massive pawn wall and plans to blast open the centre. Levy's defensive recipe: …e6 (don't take on e4!), then …Bb4 pressuring c3 and threatening to trade off White's most active piece. The …b6 + …Bb7 fianchetto activates the queenside bishop along the long diagonal. The position stays tense and double-edged but Black's pieces are coordinated.

openings.name: Scandinavian Defense (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 Bf5 Bc4 e6 Bd2 c6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Nbd7
openings.overview: Here's the dirty secret of opening theory: half of chess writing says 'don't bring your queen out early'. The Scandinavian says: 'I will, and your move'. The opening's pedigree is ancient — it appears in chess manuscripts from 1475 (one of the oldest analyzed openings in the historical record); modern revival came from Larsen and Tony Miles, who beat Karpov with the Scandinavian in 1980 (a major upset at the time). Levy made this Black's anti-1.e4 weapon for the YouTube generation because there's almost no theory beyond move 8. After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 — yes, your queen is on d5 in the open — but White's natural 3.Nc3 attacks the queen, which means White has to ASK you where she goes (3...Qa5 is the answer, hitting the e1-h4 diagonal). You've used your one queen move to gain three things: developed your queen with tempo, decoyed White's knight to c3 where it commits, and signalled you're playing fast and direct. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: Qxd5 → Qa5 is one move sequence, not two. Don't recapture with the queen on d5 thinking you'll figure out where to put her later — the only good square is a5 (the c-file gets defended by the queen, and Qa5 pins the c3-knight against the e1-king if the bishop ever comes off c1).

Bf5 BEFORE e6 is mandatory. The whole point of the Scandinavian over the Caro-Kann is that the queen comes out instead of the c-pawn — preserving the option to develop the c8-bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain. Lock the bishop in with …e6 first and you've played a Caro-Kann a tempo down.

c6 has TWO purposes. It supports an eventual …d5 break (regaining centre control) AND it prepares …Bb4 hitting the c3-knight WITH the queen on a5 pinning it — a pin-and-attack combo that wins material if White isn't careful.
Don't let White play d5. Once you've castled, watch for any moment where White's d4-d5 push could fork your queen on a5 and a piece on b5 or c6. Pre-empt with …Bd7 + …Nc6-b4 reroute if needed.
traps: After 4.Nf3 Bf5 5.Bd3 — White attacks the f5-bishop hoping for the trade. Don't trade! Move the bishop with 5...Bg6 or accept 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 only if it suits your structure. The Bd3 is a Caro-Kann move, not a Scandinavian move — White hasn't earned the bishop trade yet.
warnings: NEVER play …Qd8 retreating to the back rank — you've now wasted three tempos with the queen and you're playing the Centre Counter with no compensation. Qa5 is forced; if you didn't want Qa5, don't play the Scandinavian.

Watch for d4-d5 forks. The d4-pawn can advance to d5 attacking your queen on a5 AND something on b5 or c6 simultaneously. If your queenside isn't safe (no bishop on d7, no knight on c6 yet), don't play …c5 or …b5 that creates more targets.

variations.name: Main Line Qa5
variations.pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 Bf5 Bc4 e6 Bd2 c6 Qe2 Bb4 O-O-O Nbd7
variations.explanation: The full mainline as Levy teaches it. 3.Nc3 Qa5 places the queen on the magic square; 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 Bf5 — the bishop comes out BEFORE …e6 (this is the Scandinavian's whole point). 6.Bc4 e6 7.Bd2 (preparing O-O-O) c6 8.Qe2 Bb4! — there's the pin and attack: Bb4 hits Nc3, which is pinned by Qa5 against the king on e1. White's response: 9.O-O-O Nbd7 reaches the critical position. Both kings have committed: White queenside, Black kingside (after …Be7 and …O-O). The game becomes opposite-side castle race, but Black is fully developed and has the …c5 break ready. Levy's signature line — easy to play, easy to remember, gets you a real game from move 1.

variations.name: 2...Nf6 Scandinavian
variations.pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 d4 Nxd5 c4 Nb6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Be3 O-O Be2 Nc6 O-O e5
variations.explanation: The 'modern' Scandinavian — instead of bringing the queen out, develop the knight directly. After 2...Nf6 3.d4 (White grabs even more centre) Nxd5 4.c4 Nb6 (the knight retreats, but the c-pawn has advanced and White has committed pieces), the position takes on a Grünfeld feel: Black fianchettos with 4...g6 and 5...Bg7, fights for d4 with 9...Nc6 and the eventual 10...e5 break. The opening costs nothing positionally — Black just chose a slightly slower but more flexible setup than the queen-out main line.

openings.name: Queen's Gambit Declined (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Qc2 Nc6 a3 Qa5 Rd1 Be7
openings.overview: The QGD is the chess defence equivalent of a Volvo: not exciting, never breaks down, lasts forever. Documented in chess literature back to the 1490s but rigorously developed by Wilhelm Steinitz, Siegbert Tarrasch, and Capablanca around the turn of the 20th century — the latter making it his lifelong defence with countless tournament victories. Karpov used the QGD throughout his 1975-1985 World Championship reign. The structure (pawns on d5 + e6, knight on f6, bishop on e7, king on g8) hasn't been broken in 150 years — there's literally no opponent prep strong enough to win in the QGD by force. Levy teaches it because it lets Black focus on middlegame plans instead of opening theory. The downside: your opponent will recognise it immediately and might steer for a draw. The upside: you can't lose in 25 moves. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: Defend d5 with e6 immediately — not c6 (that's the Slav, a different opening). The …e6 move locks in your light-squared bishop on c8, which becomes the QGD's biggest practical problem to solve. Plan its escape from move 1.
The c8-bishop is your project. The three main paths: …Bd7-…Be8-…f5/g6 (slowest but safest), …b6+…Bb7 (after preparing with …a6 if needed), or trade it off via …Bg4 after Nf3. Never let it die on c8.

…c5 is the equalising break, not the winning break. After …c5 the position opens, your pieces can move, and you reach a balanced position. But …c5 played too early hangs the d5-pawn; played too late is unnecessary. The right moment is when both knights are out, both rooks are connected, and White hasn't yet played dxc5 themselves.

Against the Exchange Variation (cxd5 exd5), you're playing for the Carlsbad structure — minority attack chess. White will try b4-b5 attacking your c6-pawn; you defend with …a6 and …Rb8 + …b5 yourself, neutralising the attack and aiming for the slightly better endgame.
traps: If White plays the Exchange Variation TOO early (cxd5 before c4 has been developed), Black can answer …exd5 with confidence — the resulting IQP-shaped middlegame has Black with active pieces on c-file, e-file, and the standard …Bf5 + …Nb4-d3 attacking plan. Easier game than the QGD-proper.
warnings: NEVER take on c4 with …dxc4 in the QGD unless you have a concrete plan. Surrendering the central tension lets White play e4 with a strong centre and a tempo against your c4-pawn (White recaptures Bxc4 with development).

The c8-bishop is your problem. If you forget to plan its development, you'll reach move 20 with a piece that can only see two squares. Build every move with one eye on how the light-squared bishop eventually gets out.

variations.name: Classical 5.Bf4 Line
variations.pgn: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 Bf4 O-O e3 c5 dxc5 Bxc5 Qc2 Nc6 a3 Qa5 Rd1 Be7
variations.explanation: The modern QGD mainline against the active 5.Bf4 system. After 5...O-O 6.e3 c5! (yes, …c5 played early!) 7.dxc5 Bxc5 — Black grabs the central pawn back with the bishop, accepting White's slight space advantage but reaching active piece play. 8.Qc2 Nc6 9.a3 Qa5 (eyeing c3 and creating threats against the pinned knight) 10.Rd1 — and now the funny 10...Be7! reroutes the bishop AWAY from the active c5-square back to e7. Why? Because Be7 prepares …Nd7 + …e5 freeing the position. Looks like waste of tempo; actually a typical QGD manoeuvre — pieces reach their best squares slowly, not directly.

variations.name: Exchange Variation
variations.pgn: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7 Nf3 Re8 Qc2 c6 O-O Nf8
variations.explanation: The Exchange Variation transforms the QGD into a Carlsbad structure — Black has a pawn on c6 supporting d5, White has pawns on c5-side and the b-pawn ready to push to b5. After 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5 Be7 6.e3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.Nf3 Re8 9.Qc2 c6 10.O-O, the position settles. The plan is the Minority Attack: White will play Rab1 + b4 + b5 trying to create a weakness on c6 (after bxc6 bxc6 Black has a backward c-pawn). Black's counter: the 10...Nf8! manoeuvre reroutes the knight to g6 or e6 supporting the …f5 break or the …Bf5 light-square trade. Outplay your opponent with patient regrouping.

openings.name: Ponziani Opening (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Nd5 Qb3 Nb6 cxd4 d6 Bb5 Be6
openings.overview: The Ponziani is the ambush specialist's dream. Named after Italian theoretician Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani, who analyzed the opening in his 1769 chess book — making it one of the oldest named openings in chess; despite this 250-year pedigree, it never took off in serious tournament play and was relegated to footnote status for centuries. Only in the YouTube era have streamers and content creators (Levy among them) revived it as a surprise weapon for amateur play. 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 — and your opponent stares at the board confused. 'What is this? Is this just a slow Italian? Should I play …Nf6? …d5?' That confusion IS the opening. 3.c3 prepares d4 with extra support; if Black answers ANYTHING that doesn't immediately challenge the centre, you crash through with 4.d4 and reach a position no Italian player has prepared. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: c3 + d4 is the entire idea. The Italian Game's c3+d4 break is delayed (you only play it after castling); the Ponziani plays c3 IMMEDIATELY, threatening d4 before Black has finished developing.

Watch for the natural-looking 3…Nf6 — this is what 95% of opponents play. Then 4.d4! and if 4…Nxe4 5.d5! kicks the c6-knight AND attacks the e4-knight (since it's no longer defended by Nc6). Black's pieces tangle and material is lost.

Against the principled 3…d5, your answer is the unusual 4.Qa4! — pinning the c6-knight to the d-pawn. This isn't a queen sortie like the Scandinavian; it's a specific tactical resource that disrupts Black's whole development.
The Ponziani has no theory at the club level — your opponents are playing on intuition while you're playing on preparation. Even if engines call the position equal, the tempo advantage is real.
traps: After 3…Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4?? 5.d5! the c6-knight has to move (no defender), but wherever it goes (5…Ne7 or 5…Nb8), White plays 6.Qa4+ winning the e4-knight. Pure pin-and-fork tactics from move 5.
warnings: Be ready for 3…d5! — the principled equaliser. After 4.Qa4 Nf6 5.Nxe5 Bd6 6.Nxc6 bxc6, Black has the bishop pair AND active piece play. Engines call it equal; if you don't know the line, you'll be on the back foot.

NEVER play d4 without first playing c3. If you skip c3 (or play d4 too soon), Black's 4…exd4 5.Nxd4 reaches an Open Game where the c3-pawn would have been useful — you've simply played a worse Scotch.

variations.name: Main Line 3...Nf6 4.d4
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 Nd5 Qb3 Nb6 cxd4 d6 Bb5 Be6
variations.explanation: The sharpest Ponziani line — Black accepts the gambit and grabs e4 with the knight. White responds with 5.d5 attacking the c6-knight. Black's only real try is 5...Bc5! threatening Bxf2+ with discovered tactics. After 6.dxc6 (winning a pawn) Bxf2+! 7.Ke2 — the king walks into the centre, but it's actually safe there. Why? Because after 7...bxc6 (Black recovers the pawn via the open b-file), the position is theoretically balanced but practically explosive. White has a king on e2 looking exposed but with all pieces ready to develop; Black has a slight material advantage (gained the e4-pawn) but a wrecked structure (doubled c-pawns). The position favours whoever has studied it more. If you've watched Levy's video — that's you.

variations.name: 3...d5 Central Counter
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c3 d5 Qa4 Nf6 Nxe5 Bd6 Nxc6 bxc6 d3 O-O Be2 Re8 Nd2
variations.explanation: The principled refutation — Black challenges the centre immediately. White's reply is the brilliant 4.Qa4! pinning the c6-knight against the e8-king (via the diagonal a4-d7-e8 with the d-pawn on d5 blocking). Black plays 4...Nf6 developing, but White grabs the loose e5-pawn with 5.Nxe5! — possible because c6 is pinned. Black tries 5...Bd6 hitting the knight on e5, but after 6.Nxc6 bxc6, White has won a pawn. The structural cost: Black has doubled c-pawns and the bishop pair. Theoretically balanced (Black has dynamic compensation), but at amateur level the extra pawn often holds.

openings.name: Fantasy Variation vs Caro-Kann (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4 e5 Nf3 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 O-O Bc5
openings.overview: Levy made the Fantasy Variation famous on YouTube — but it has older roots. The 3.f3 move was experimented with by Hungarian GM Geza Maroczy in the early 1900s as a surprise weapon, and David Bronstein later employed it in his unique, creative style. It remained an obscure sideline until modern theoreticians revived it for the online era. Every Caro-Kann player you face has prepared the Classical (3.Nc3) and the Advance (3.e5). Almost nobody has prepared the Fantasy (3.f3). The numbers don't lie: at 1500-2000 level, the surprise alone produces a +0.4 rating-point swing — that's the difference between a draw and a win. The system works because 3.f3 supports a massive central pawn duo while keeping White's options open: you can play for a positional crush after 3...e6, or accept the gambit-style mess after 3...dxe4 4.fxe4. Either way, you're playing memorised lines and Black is improvising. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: The pawn structure e4-d4-f3 dominates the centre. Don't trade these pawns lightly — the d-pawn is the most important; if Black ever plays …e5 hitting it, support with Nf3 rather than dxe5 (which simplifies and helps Black).

Bc4 is mandatory, NOT Bd3. The c4-bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal is the whole reason f3 makes positional sense — the bishop targets f7, AND the f3-pawn defends the e4-pawn, freeing the bishop from defensive duties.

If Black plays the principled …e5 hitting d4, you HAVE to play Nf3 calmly (not dxe5 which would help Black). After 5.Nf3 exd4 you're a pawn down but you have huge development and the open f-file — full gambit compensation.

Against the solid …e6, the centre stays closed and you play for the kingside attack with Bf4, Qd3 (or Qd2), O-O-O, then g4-g5 like an open Sicilian English Attack. Just remember which side castled — your king on c1 has to be solid before you commit pawns forward.
traps: If Black plays 3…dxe4 4.fxe4 e5?? — the natural-looking central counter — White just plays 5.dxe5! winning a clean pawn. Black's queen has no good square (5...Qxd1+ 6.Kxd1 actually favours White — the e5-pawn cramps Black). Black's only sound reply to 4.fxe4 is …e5 followed by …exd4 (gambit-style), not the simple 4…e5 grab.
After 3…e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 (the natural pin) — your move is 5.Bf4! NOT Bd2. The Bf4 keeps the central tension AND develops to a more active square; after 5...Nf6 6.e5 cramps the f6-knight back.
warnings: f3 only works after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 — never play f3 in OTHER Caro-Kann move orders (like the Classical with 2.Nc3 first), where the f3-pawn would just weaken the kingside without preparing a central duo.

Be ready for the …Bg4 pin pattern. The f3-pawn weakens White's defence of the e4-pawn AND blocks the natural Nf3 development; if you ever play Nf3 with the queen still on d1, the …Bg4 pin is real and can lose material to a follow-up …Bxf3.

variations.name: Main Line 3...dxe4 4.fxe4
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4 e5 Nf3 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 O-O Bc5
variations.explanation: Levy's main attacking line — and this one's a real fight. Black accepts the central exchange with 3...dxe4 4.fxe4, then immediately challenges your remaining centre with 4...e5. You defend the d4-pawn with 5.Nf3 (NOT 5.dxe5 which gives Black equality) — accepting that you'll lose a pawn for development. Black grabs with 5...exd4. Now your plan: 6.Bc4 (NOT Bd3 — the c4-bishop is the heart of the system) Nf6 7.O-O Bc5 — both sides develop aggressively. The position now: you're down a pawn, but you have the open f-file (rook on f1 ready), the Bc4 aimed at f7, the e4-pawn cramping Black, and Black hasn't castled. The compensation is real and concrete. Aim for tactics around the f-file and the b3-square if Black plays …b5 hitting the bishop.

variations.name: Solid 3...e6
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Bf4 Ne7 Qd3 b6
variations.explanation: Black plays the safe 3...e6 declining the central tension. You respond 4.Nc3 Bb4 (the natural pin) 5.Bf4! — the active bishop development that keeps central tension AND eyes c7 and e5 squares. Black tries to challenge with 5...Ne7 (heading to g6 supporting f5 or trying to trade your bishop) 6.Qd3 b6 — Black fianchettos hoping to put pressure on e4 via …Bb7. The position is a closed centre middlegame; your plan is to castle queenside, play g4, push pawns toward the kingside while Black tries to find counterplay against e4. Slower than the main line but easier to play if you don't like tactical chess.

variations.name: Aggressive 3...g6
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Be3 dxe4 fxe4 Nf6 Nf3 O-O Bd3
variations.explanation: Black tries the unusual 3...g6 + …Bg7 fianchetto — a Pirc-style setup. You develop naturally with 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Be3 (NOT Bf4 here — Be3 supports d4 and prepares queenside castling) dxe4 6.fxe4 (recover the e-pawn) Nf6 7.Nf3 O-O 8.Bd3 — only NOW you can play Bd3, because the e4-pawn is solidly defended by Nc3 + Nf3 + Bd3. Bd3 points at h7 with attacking ideas; the centre e4+d4 holds; Black's fianchetto bishop on g7 bites on the d4-pawn defended by everything. White has a comfortable structural edge.

openings.name: Milner-Barry Gambit vs French (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4 cxd4 Bd7 O-O Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc3 a6 Qe2 Ne7 Kh1
openings.overview: Here's the deal with the French Defence: if you let Black play it on their terms, they reach a structure they've studied since they were a kid and you spend the next 60 moves chipping at a granite wall. The Milner-Barry says: not today. Named after Stuart Milner-Barry — British chess master AND Bletchley Park codebreaker who worked alongside Alan Turing on cracking the Enigma — this gambit was his pet anti-French weapon in the 1930s-40s. After 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 (the Advance) c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3, when Black plays the natural 5...Qb6 hitting d4, you don't defend the pawn — you sacrifice it with 6.Bd3! Black is invited to grab it; if they do, you've traded one pawn for total development supremacy. If they don't, you've reached a position with the better-placed pieces. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: The d4-pawn is the bait. After Black plays …Qb6 hitting it, you respond Bd3 — NOT Nc3 (which blocks the queen's defence) and NOT Qd2 (passive). The point: Bd3 develops AND prepares O-O; if Black takes the d4-pawn, your lead in development is worth more than a pawn.

The standard sequence after Black accepts: 6...cxd4 7.cxd4 Nxd4 8.Nxd4 Qxd4 9.Nc3 — Black's queen is now in the open, the Nc3 develops with tempo, and Black is forced into defensive moves while you finish development.

The e5-pawn is your structural ally for the whole game. It cramps Black's c8-bishop (locked behind …b6 or …f6), it controls f6 and d6, and it supports a future f4-f5 kingside attack. Defend it like a king.

After 9.Nc3, look for Black's natural 9...a6 (preparing …b5) and respond 10.Qe2 + 11.Kh1 — the king tucks away while you prepare Rd1 piling on the queen. Black has the extra pawn but spends the next 15 moves trying to consolidate.
traps: If Black gets really greedy with 9...Qxb2?? — punishment via 10.Nc3 Qb4 (only square — Qa3 hangs to Nb5) 11.Rb1 Qa5 12.Nb5! — the knight forks ideas (Nc7+, Nd6+) and Black's queen is in serious trouble. The b2-pawn is double-poisoned.
warnings: ONLY play this against the Advance French (after 3.e5 — Black has committed to …c5). It does NOT work against the Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) or the Classical (3.Nc3 Nf6) — those need different systems entirely.

If Black declines the gambit with 6...Bd7 (instead of 6...cxd4), DON'T try to hold the d-pawn — just develop with 7.O-O and play a normal Advance French. The Milner-Barry's whole point is the gambit; if Black declines, accept the equal middlegame.

variations.name: Main Gambit Line
variations.pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4 cxd4 Bd7 O-O Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc3 a6 Qe2 Ne7 Kh1
variations.explanation: The full Milner-Barry. Black accepts the pawn sacrifice with 6...cxd4 7.cxd4 Bd7 (developing first, planning Nxd4 next) 8.O-O Nxd4! (the moment of truth — Black grabs the pawn) 9.Nxd4 Qxd4. White is down a pawn but plays 10.Nc3 with tempo on the queen, 10...a6 (preventing Nb5 fork) 11.Qe2 (preparing Rd1 + Rad1) 11...Ne7 (Black develops) 12.Kh1 — the king safety prophylaxis before the attack begins. Position: Black is up a pawn but undeveloped (rook still on h8, king on e8, bishop on f8); White has every piece in optimal place. The next 5 moves are forced for Black — defend or die — while White picks up tempos building the attack.

variations.name: Black Declines with Bd7
variations.pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 Bd7 O-O cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Nc3 Qb6
variations.explanation: Sometimes Black plays 6...Bd7 first (developing) rather than 6...cxd4 immediately. After 7.O-O cxd4 8.cxd4 Nxd4 9.Nxd4 Qxd4 10.Nc3 — same gambit position reached via different move order. Black's only difference: the bishop is already on d7 (so 10...Qb6 retreating the queen is the standard plan). The end position favours White's better development, but Black has the extra pawn AND has avoided the worst of the Milner-Barry attack by retreating the queen early.

variations.name: Anti-French 3.e5 Advance
variations.pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Nh6 Bd3 cxd4 cxd4 Nf5 Bxf5 exf5 Nc3 Be6 O-O Be7
variations.explanation: When Black tries the unusual 5...Nh6 (heading to f5 to challenge your light-squared bishop), accept the trade: 6.Bd3 cxd4 7.cxd4 Nf5 8.Bxf5! exf5 — Black has doubled f-pawns and a cramped position. White's central pawns plus open structure for the rooks give a long-term positional edge. Black's …Be6 + …Be7 development is passive; you're playing for the win on positional grounds rather than the usual gambit fireworks.

openings.name: Anti-Sicilian Rossolimo (GothamChess)
openings.pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 Re1 a6 Bf1 d5 exd5 Nxd5 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4
openings.overview: The Sicilian is the most theoretical opening in chess. The Rossolimo says: 'Don't play that game.' Named after Russian-born American GM Nicolas Rossolimo, who systematized the 3.Bb5 approach in the 1940s-50s and used it throughout his career to score remarkable results against the Sicilian. Magnus Carlsen has played it consistently throughout his career — both as a winning weapon against weaker opposition AND as a peace offering against the best, since the resulting positions reward technical skill over memorization. After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6, White plays 3.Bb5 — pinning the c6-knight against Black's development. Now there's no Open Sicilian. No Najdorf preparation. Black has to play their own game against a setup that 9 out of 10 Sicilian players haven't studied beyond move 7. You'll lose to a 2200; you'll crush a 1500. Levy is an attacking, middlegame-decisive player — his games are built to win in the opening and the middlegame, not grind long endings — so this repertoire is deepest on the opening and middlegame plans, with endgame theory shown only where his actual games reach a decisive ending.
keyIdeas: Bb5 is the heart of the system. It pins the c6-knight (preventing standard …e5 pushes), prepares Bxc6 (creating doubled pawns on c6), and develops the bishop to a useful square. Don't trade it lightly — the bishop on b5 is the entire opening.

Decide early: trade or retreat. Against …a6, your two choices are 4.Bxc6 (commit to the structural game — doubled pawns for Black, two bishops for you) or 4.Ba4 (keep the bishop, play for Italian-style positions). Bxc6 is more concrete; Ba4 keeps options open.

The d4 break still works in the Rossolimo — but on YOUR terms. After castling, you can play d4 in one move (one of White's structural advantages over an Open Sicilian where d4 happens on move 3). The IQP positions favour White because the c6-pawn is doubled and weak.

Avoids Najdorf/Dragon/Sveshnikov/Taimanov/Kan completely. The Sicilian player has spent years studying open lines — none of that helps in the Rossolimo. You're playing a different game and they're improvising from move 7.
traps: After 3...g6? (the fianchetto attempt) — Levy's video has 200K views on this. Play 4.Bxc6! bxc6 (or dxc6) and Black's structure is permanently damaged. The dark-squared bishop wanted to go to g7 long-diagonal, but now the diagonal targets nothing because the e5-pawn is gone. Pure structural punishment.
warnings: The Rossolimo ONLY works against 2…Nc6. If Black plays 2…d6 (Najdorf move order) or 2…e6 (Taimanov move order), you can't play Bb5+ because there's nothing to pin. Have a different anti-Sicilian (like the Closed Sicilian with c3 or the Alapin) in reserve.

Don't trade Bxc6 reflexively — sometimes the pin is the point. If Black hasn't played …a6 yet and you have other useful moves (O-O, Re1, d4 prep), use the pin as a long-term asset rather than cashing it in immediately.

variations.name: Rossolimo 3.Bb5 e6
variations.pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 O-O Nge7 Re1 a6 Bf1 d5 exd5 Nxd5 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4
variations.explanation: The flagship Rossolimo line. Black plays 3...e6 (preparing …d5 to challenge the centre) and …Nge7 (the knight goes to e7 supporting …d5). You set up with 4.O-O Nge7 5.Re1 a6 — and now the unusual retreat 6.Bf1! The bishop goes back to f1 to keep the b1-h7 diagonal open AND get out of the way of a future d4 push. After 6...d5 (Black's break) 7.exd5 Nxd5 8.d4! cxd4 9.Nxd4 Nxd4 10.Qxd4, you've reached an IQP-style position with the queen centralised, knight on d4, and Black's pieces still scrambled. The bishop on f1 will come out later to a more active square once the position settles. Classic Rossolimo squeeze.

variations.name: Rossolimo 3.Bb5 g6
variations.pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 Re1 e5 Bxc6 dxc6 d3
variations.explanation: Against the fianchetto setup, the Rossolimo gets concrete. Black plays 3...g6 + 4...Bg7 preparing to put the bishop on the long diagonal. You respond 5.Re1 e5 (Black tries to lock the centre supporting the fianchetto) 6.Bxc6! dxc6 (Black recaptures with the d-pawn to keep the central pawn structure) 7.d3 — locking in a long-term structural advantage. Black has doubled c-pawns and the half-open d-file is yours. The bishop on g7 looks active but it's biting on YOUR central pawn on d3 — defended. Position favours the better long-term technique.

variations.name: Accelerated Pawn Storm (Carlsen-inspired)
variations.pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 e6 Bxc6 bxc6 d3 d5 e5 Ne7 b3 Ng6 Bb2
variations.explanation: Magnus Carlsen popularised this approach — trade on c6 IMMEDIATELY after Black's …e6 setup. After 4.Bxc6 bxc6 (Black takes with the b-pawn keeping the c-file under control) 5.d3 d5 6.e5! — you push the e-pawn to cramp Black, the c-pawn structure (now doubled and weak) is a permanent target. White's plan: develop with Nbd2, h3, O-O, then attack on the kingside while Black struggles to find counterplay with the broken queenside. Carlsen has won multiple games in this line at the highest level.

openings.name: Caro-Kann Defense (Naroditsky)
openings.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 c5 dxc5 e6 Nf3 Bxc5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Nge7
openings.overview: This is the Caro-Kann Naroditsky has actually played thousands of times — not a textbook diagram, his ACTUAL repertoire. The line he plays vs the Advance Variation (e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 c5!) is the modern c5 break, also known as the Botvinnik-Carls Defense. In his 3,546 Caro-Kann games on chess.com he scores 64% with this — including against opponents rated over 3300. The whole opening rests on three ideas: (1) the c6-pawn is a wedge supporting d5 forever, (2) when White attacks on the flank we strike in the centre, and (3) the …Bg4 pin against an Nf3 knight is a recurring tactical motif we look for in every variation. The Caro isn't a defensive opening — it's a counter-attacking one. We let White over-commit, we keep our structure clean, and then we punish.
keyIdeas: The c6-pawn is not a weakness — it's a wedge. It supports d5 forever and lets us recapture toward the centre. The whole Caro philosophy comes down to this: we give White the early development tempo because the structure we earn is worth more. When you hear 'doubled pawns' (in the Classical's f-file) or 'passive bishop' (the c8-bishop), remember: those are static features. The game is decided by what we DO with them, not what they look like on move 5.

When White plays on the flank, we counter in the centre. This is the rule that decides 90% of our middlegames. If White goes for h4-h5 on the kingside (Advance Variation) or pawn-storms with f3/g4, we hit them with …c5 or …e5 in the centre BEFORE the wing attack arrives. The flank attack only works if the centre is closed; we keep it open or open it ourselves.

The wishlist method works here perfectly. Before you calculate, ask: what's my IDEAL position 5 moves from now? Usually it's: bishop on f5 or g4, knight on d7 or f6, queen on c7, rooks coordinated on the d- and e-files. Work backwards from that picture — that's how we find the right move. Don't search for tactics; search for the SHAPE we want, and the tactics will appear when the shape is right.

The light-squared bishop is the question mark of the Caro. It wants to be ACTIVE — Bf5 in the Advance mainlines, Bg4 in the Exchange and Classical, or rerouting via Bd7-Bc8-Bf5 in slower setups. The wrong answer is leaving it locked behind the pawn chain. The right move depends on White's move order: against c3 + Bd3 we play …Bg4 early; against the Bd3 + Nf3 setup we time …Bg4 to threaten Bxf3 (doubling White's pawns); in the Advance with c5 it stays home until we've untangled with …Bxc5, …Nc6, …Nge7, and emerges late via the kingside. The rule: don't let the c8-bishop be a tombstone.
traps: If White plays an early Bg5 (in the Classical, after our …dxe4 and …Nf6), the …h6 push is not a question — it's a demand. White MUST commit (retreat to h4, trade on f6, or pretend nothing happened). The trick: if they retreat Bh4, our …g5 is now playable because their knight on f3 is committed and the dark squares we 'weaken' are squares we control with our bishop and queen anyway. Don't fear the loose look — the geometry favours us.

Against the Fantasy (f3), the GREEDY move dxe4 fxe4 e5 Nf3 looks like it lets White off the hook — but after Nf3 exd4 Nxd4 we have a fluid centre and White's e4-pawn is hanging in space, defended by no minor pieces yet. The trap is for WHITE: if they try to defend e4 with Bd3 or Qe2 too soon, we get …Nf6 with tempo on e4 and a comfortable game where their early f3 hurt them more than it helped.
warnings: Don't auto-play …Bf5 in the Advance. It's the textbook move (Bf5 vs the Advance Variation), but in the c5 line we play, the bishop belongs on g4 or stays on c8 until the …c5 / …Nc6 / …Nge7 setup is complete. Premature …Bf5 in the Botvinnik-Carls line lets White play h4-h5 with tempo on the bishop, and we end up dancing instead of developing. Trust the move order: c5 first, then pieces.

In the Two Knights (Nc3 line), don't get cute with early …dxe4 + …Nf6 hoping for a Petroff-style game. White's Nf3 + Nxe4 setup is FINE for them in those structures. Our move order — …d5, accept the trades, develop quietly — is the line that gives us the 64% score. The 'sharp' alternatives sacrifice the comfort we earned with the move order.

Watch the diagonal a2-g8 in the Exchange. After …Bg4 our king has castled short and White's Bd3 is staring through Bg4 at h7. If you ever let White trade dark-squared bishops AND keep the Bd3 alive, the h7 weakness becomes a real attacking target. Rule: in the Exchange, trade light-squared bishops (your Bg4 for their Nf3), and keep the dark-squared bishops on if possible. The dark squares around our king are not the issue; the light squares are.

variations.name: Two Knights Variation (Nc3)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Qe2 Nxe4 Qxe4 Nd7 Bc4 Nf6 Ne5 e6 Qe2 b5 Bb3 Qc7
variations.explanation: When White plays Nc3 on move 2, they're sidestepping the main Caro mainlines and inviting a piece game. The point of this line for us as Black: play …d5 straight away, let the centre trade, and develop fast. After the early piece trades we end up with Bb3 vs …b5 / …Qc7 — a comfortable position where our queen and pieces are coordinated and White's bishop on b3 is staring at granite (the b5-pawn). From here we look to finish development with …Bb7 and …Be7, castle short, and consolidate. The number-one rule against the Two Knights: don't get cute, just play sound moves and reach a balanced middlegame. The position rewards patience — White ran out of useful moves first.

variations.name: King's Indian Attack (Nf3)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 Nf3 d5 d3 Qc7 Nc3 dxe4 dxe4 e5 Bc4
variations.explanation: Against the KIA-style Nf3 + d3 setup, the trick is recognising what White is doing: they're not playing a real opening, they're playing a system. So we don't have to fear sharp theoretical lines — what we have to fear is letting them build slow comfort. Our answer: …d5, then …Qc7 to discourage e5, and when White trades on d5 we recapture with the e-pawn or open the centre with …e5 ourselves. Result: piece-for-piece development, no structural mess, a comfortable middle-game with the bishop pair often becoming ours. We score 62% here in real play. Don't overextend — the win comes from playing accurate, principled moves while White wanders.

variations.name: Exchange Variation (exd5)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 Bd3 Nf6 c3 Bg4 Qb3 Qc7 h3
variations.explanation: When White trades on d5, they're trying to bleed the tension out of the position and reach a symmetrical pawn structure where their slightly easier development gives an edge. Our scheme — straight from the data — is the early …Bg4 development, …Qc7 covering b7, and quiet piece play. Bd3 has nothing to attack; the c3 / Qb3 / h3 plan looks active but accomplishes very little; we retreat the bishop (Bh5 keeps the diagonal alive, Be6 reroutes to f5 later) and finish development with …e6, …Nc6, …Bd6, …O-O. The point: a symmetrical position is only equal if both sides develop equally. We make sure ours is one tempo faster. 64% score in his actual games — the Exchange isn't dangerous, it's tedious for White.

variations.name: Classical Variation (Nc3)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Nxf6+ exf6 c3 Bd6 Bd3 O-O Qc2 Re8+ Ne2 h5
variations.explanation: The Classical Caro is the line where Black accepts doubled f-pawns (after …Nxf6 or …exf6) in exchange for active development and the half-open e-file. White's Bd3 + Qc2 setup is the standard plan — they want h-pawn pressure on our king. Our reply: don't let them. After castling we play …Re8+ to chase the knight (forcing Ne2, a passive square) and then …h5 ourselves, freezing their h-pawn before it lands on h4. The doubled f-pawns are NOT a weakness — they're a wedge. We control e5 forever and the open lines for our rook on e8 are real. Score: 62% — equal-but-active for Black, exactly what we want against a respected mainline.

variations.name: Fantasy Variation (f3)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4 e5
variations.explanation: The Fantasy is White's attempt to build a massive centre and just shove us off the board. The refutation: don't let the centre stand. After f3 we play …dxe4 (open the file), fxe4 …e5 (challenge it back), and immediately White has a decision — push d5 and lock the position with an awkward pawn chain, or trade on e5 and accept that their f3 was just a wasted tempo. Either way we equalise comfortably. Our score in the data is 75% — the highest of any Caro variation he plays — because White's whole premise (intimidation) collapses the moment we play forcing chess. Don't overthink this one: …dxe4, …e5, develop, win.

variations.name: Modern Defense Transposition (d4 g6)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 d5
variations.explanation: Sometimes when we hit the Caro move-order against a d4 player who wasn't expecting it, the cleanest game is to transpose — fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, get a Pirc/Modern structure with the c-pawn already on c6 (which is FINE, not bad — it supports …d5 perfectly). After …Bg7 and …d5 we have a hybrid setup that's familiar to Modern players but with one extra useful tempo. White's pieces aim at a wall: the Bg7, the c6-d5 pawn chain, the well-defended king. 68% score in the data — White rarely plays this critically because they expected a Caro and got a Modern.

variations.name: Advance Variation (3.e5 c5)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 c5 dxc5 e6 Nf3 Bxc5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O Nge7 Nbd2 Ng6 Nb3 Bb6 Re1 Qc7 a4 a6
variations.explanation: The Advance Variation with immediate ...c5 counter-strike — 528 games in his archive, 55% score. Modern Caro theory says ...c5 is stronger than the classical ...Bf5 because it challenges White's centre directly. The 22-ply spine walks through the dxc5 trade, the Bxc5 recapture, and the Nge7-Ng6 reroute targeting the f4-e5 dark squares. The Black knight on g6 + bishop pair + open c-file gives steady positional pressure that converts in the R+min+P endgame.

variations.name: Advance Variation (3.e5 Bf5)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nf3 e6 Be2 c5 Be3
variations.explanation: The classical Advance treatment: ...Bf5 developing the light-square bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain (the Caro's structural advantage over the French Defense). 53 games — less common than the immediate ...c5 but still well-tested. The Bf5 supports the kingside while we prepare ...e6 + ...c5 break with full classical development. White's Be2 setup avoids the tactical Bd3 lines.

variations.name: Panov-Botvinnik Attack (4.c4)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Bg5 Be6 Be2 Qa5 c5 Ne4 Bd2 Nxd2 Qxd2 g6 Nf3 Bg7
variations.explanation: The Panov-Botvinnik Attack — White's most aggressive treatment after the Exchange. 99 games, 51% win rate. White accepts an Isolated Queen's Pawn structure in exchange for active piece play; Black answers with the Nf6+Nc6+Bg5 pin response. The ...Be6+Qa5+...Ne4 sequence simplifies the position favorably, and Black ends with the fianchetto setup + bishop pair + active queen.

variations.name: d3 Sideline (2.d3)
variations.pgn: e4 c6 d3 d5 Nd2 e5 g3 Bd6 Bg2 Nf6 Ngf3 O-O O-O Re8 b3 a5 a4 Na6 Bb2 Nb4 Re1 dxe4 Nxe4 Nxe4 dxe4
variations.explanation: White's quiet 2.d3 sideline — 158 games, 71% win rate (Black's BEST scoring Caro variation in the corpus). White treats the opening as a KIA-reversed Sicilian; Black answers with central ...e5 + classical ...Bd6 + ...Nbd7 development. The reversed-Sicilian-Scheveningen structure converts easily because Black has the active piece play AND the central simplification favors Black's coordination.

trapLines.name: Qe2 wastes a tempo (Two Knights KIA setup)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Qe2 Nxe4 Qxe4 e6
trapLines.explanation: Mined from his archive — 170 games (his biggest Caro trap pattern) where opponents played Qe2 instead of the principled Nxf6+/Ng3 in the Two Knights KIA setup. The Qe2 blocks the f1-bishop AND lets ...Nxe4 Qxe4 e6 develop with tempo. Named 2700+ victim: penguingm1 (3165).

trapLines.name: h3 hands Black the bishop pair (KIA Bg4 line)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6
trapLines.explanation: Mined from 29 games. After the standard ...Bg4 pin, White's h3 forces the trade Black wanted — bishop pair + structurally healthier kingside go to Black. Named 2700+ victims: GM_dmitrij (2940), Mykola-Bortnyk (2953), wonderfultime (2905).

trapLines.name: dxe4 → Qxd1+ exposes White's king (d3 line)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 Nf3 d5 d3 dxe4 dxe4 Qxd1+ Kxd1
trapLines.explanation: Mined from 26 games. In the quiet 2.d3 sideline, after ...dxe4 White's recapture with the d-pawn (instead of the knight) loses to the immediate Qxd1+ queen trade — forcing the king to d1 where it's permanently exposed. Named 2700+ victims: BrandonJacobson (3136), TLTLTLTLTLTL (3207), Kriari (2910).

trapLines.name: Bd3 voluntary trade in the Exchange Caro
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 Nf3 Nf6 h3 Bf5 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3
trapLines.explanation: Mined from 20 games. After Exchange Caro Nf3+h3+Bd3, White's voluntary bishop trade lets Black equalise cleanly with no problem pieces — the Exchange's drawishness favours Black who has zero risk. Named 2700+ victims: Oleksandr_Bortnyk (3278), BrandonJacobson (2873), Mykola-Bortnyk (3135).

trapLines.name: Nxf6+ premature trade (Classical Caro)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Nxf6+ exf6 c3 Bg4
trapLines.explanation: Mined from 6 games. After Classical Nc3+Nxe4 setup, White's premature Nxf6+ wastes a tempo because Black's ...exf6 opens the e-file AND ...Bg4 develops with the pin. Named 2700+ victims: Arambai (3161), Oleksandr_Bortnyk (3148).

trapLines.name: The …Bg4 Pin When White Develops Nf3 Early
trapLines.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3 Bg4 c3 e6 Qb3 Qc7 h3 Bxf3 gxf3
trapLines.explanation: When White's move order puts Nf3 BEFORE Bd3 — a frequent transposition — the …Bg4 develops with the pin live. After the natural Qb3 attacks b7 and Black covers with …Qc7, White's h3 forces the trade: …Bxf3 gxf3 wrecks the kingside pawn structure permanently. From here Black completes development with …Bd6, …O-O, …Rfe8 and a long-term structural edge: White's king is exposed, their pieces lack coordination, and the doubled f-pawns create a static weakness Black plays against for the rest of the game.

warningLines.name: Premature …Bf5 in the Advance c5 Line
warningLines.pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 h4 h6 g4 Bd7
warningLines.explanation: Why we play …c5 first, not …Bf5. After e5, the textbook move is …Bf5 — but in the line Naroditsky plays we instead play …c5 to challenge the centre. The reason: if we go …Bf5 first, White plays the h4-h5 / g4 plan and our bishop spends the next 10 moves dancing — Bd7-c8-d7 — while White seizes space. After the …Bd7 retreat shown here, Black is two tempi down on development and the position is just unpleasant.

openings.name: Alapin Sicilian (Naroditsky)
openings.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 d5 exd6 Qxd6 O-O
openings.overview: The c3 anti-Sicilian — Naroditsky's most-played weapon vs c5 (2,752 games, 73.8% score). The whole point is move three: d4, supported by the c3-pawn, building a classical centre instead of letting Black drag us into Sicilian theory. We score 73.8% across nearly 3,000 games here for one reason — opponents prepared for the Open Sicilian get a structural game instead, and they're outclassed positionally before they realize they're not in a sharp fight.
keyIdeas: c3 supports d4. The whole opening is setup for ONE move. After e4 c5 c3, we WILL play d4 on move 3 (or move 4 after Black declares), and the centre will be ours. Black's …d5 challenges are met with a pawn-trade that opens the position favorably.

Nf6 gets kicked to d5, then chased to b6. Black's natural development is punished by tempo — we push e5, the knight bounces to d5, our Bc4 hits it, and they retreat to b6. We've gained two tempi while developing pieces naturally.

a4-a5-a6 cramps Black's queenside. After the typical trades around move 10, we play a4 starting the queenside crawl. Black's pawn on a7 becomes weak, the b6-knight has nowhere to go, and the c-file is half-open for us forever.

Trade bishops on e6 when offered. Black's …Be6 is the standard development — we trade with Bxe6, removing Black's good piece and keeping our knight + bishop pair. Long-term structural advantage every time.
traps: If Black plays the careless Nf6?? attacking e4 again, we already have e5 and the knight on f6 is en prise — that's why move-order matters. Black must play the central d5 or accept the cramped Nf6 / e6 lines.
After the typical Bb3 d5 Black tries to win the pawn back with Nxe5? — but Nxe5 Qa5+ Nc3 wins on tempi; Black has to retreat the queen and we keep the extra pawn.
warnings: Don't push d4 too early. After c3, we must wait until Black's centre is committed (Nf6 e5 ...) before pushing d4. Premature d4? cxd4 cxd4 d5! gives Black equality immediately.

Don't trade Bb3 voluntarily. The bishop on b3 is staring at f7 for the rest of the game; it's our best piece. Let Black come to us — if they offer …Be6, we trade them; if they don't, the bishop stays and we attack with it.

variations.name: 2…d5 Open Variation
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Na3 Nc6 Be3 cxd4 Nb5 Qd7 Nbxd4 Be7 Nxc6 Qxc6 Ne5 Qe4 Bb5+ Kf8 Nf3
variations.explanation: Black's second-most-played reply (783 games, 71.3% for him, 66.3% for us — our lowest of the major lines). The Na3-Nb5 outpost wins tempi on the queen, the central trades open the position, and the Bb5+ check fixes Black's king on f8 for the rest of the game. R+minor+P endgames (27.4% of decisive games here) convert the structural edge.

variations.name: 2…e6 French-Style
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 e6 d4 d5 e5 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 Bd3 cxd4 O-O dxc3 Nxc3 a6 Re1 Bc5 Ng5
variations.explanation: Black plays a French-Advance setup with …e6/…d5 (344 games, 74% score). We cramp with e5, accept the pawn sacrifice via O-O before recapture, and end up with open files + bishop pair vs Black's locked-in pieces. The Ng5 jump threatens f7 tactics that Black struggles to defend at speed.

variations.name: 2…d6 Mainline
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 d6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 h3 Bg7 Nf3 O-O Bd3 Nc6 O-O
variations.explanation: Black's quiet 2…d6 reply (173 games, his BEST-scoring variation at 80.6% — the highest Alapin sub-line). Black avoids commitment, we claim the centre immediately, transpose into a KID-reversed where WE have the extra tempo. Slow positional pressure with h3 + Bd3 + O-O setup; we win via the eventual e4-e5 or d4-d5 break.

variations.name: 2…g6 Hyper-Dragon
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 g6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Nc3 Nxd5 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 Bg7 Nf3 O-O
variations.explanation: Hyper-Accelerated Dragon (125 games, 79.6% for him). Black fianchettoes immediately; we transpose into a Panov-style position with Bc4-Bb3 attacking from the same diagonal as in the main spine. Same plan, same piece coordination, different move order.

variations.name: 2…Nc6 Line
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 Qd8 Bd3 Nf6 O-O Be7 a3
variations.explanation: The 2…Nc6 line (116 games, 86.2% for him — his HIGHEST Alapin score). Black tries the Scandi-style simplification, but Nc3 gains a tempo on the queen and forces …Qd8 — the queen returns home, two tempi lost, structural game converted in the endgame. R+minor+P = 33.7% of decisive games.

variations.name: Spine 4…d6 Bc4 Gambit
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nb6 e6 Nxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 exf7+ Kxf7 Qxc4+ d5 Qf4+ Kg8 d4
variations.explanation: Inside the main 2…Nf6 spine — Black's 4…d6 challenge to e5 (394 games, 70.3%). Per Gordima's distillation, this is Naroditsky's distinguishing Alapin treatment: the Bb5+ → Bc4 transposition. We ignore the e5-pawn, sacrifice with e6 + exf7+ to break the king cover, recover material via Qa4+ → Qxc4+, end up with no material loss + Black's king on g8 without a pawn shield.

variations.name: Spine 4…e6 IQP Lines
variations.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe2 Bd7 Rd1 Bc6 Nc3 Nxc3 bxc3
variations.explanation: Inside the main 2…Nf6 spine — Black's quieter 4…e6 reply (185 games, 72.4%). White transposes into a Panov-Botvinnik-style IQP middlegame with central control + open files. The Nc3 jump + Nxc3/bxc3 trade gives doubled c-pawns but also the open b-file + bishop pair — three pluses for one minor weakness.

trapLines.name: Nc3 Queen-Tempo (2…Nc6 Line)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nf3 e6 Nc3 Qd8
trapLines.explanation: After Black's 2…Nc6 transposes into a Scandi-style trade with …Qxd5, the simple Nc3 develops a piece AND gains tempo on the queen — Black's only safe square is …Qd8, the queen's starting square. Two tempi lost from the queen-out gambit, structural game decided. 86.2% score in 116 games tells you Black's tries don't work at amateur level.

trapLines.name: Bc4-Gambit + exf7+ (Nc6 block fails, 62 games incl. Hans Niemann 3161)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Nb6 e6 Nxc4 Qa4+ Nc6 exf7+ Kxf7 Qxc4+ e6 O-O Qf6
trapLines.explanation: Naroditsky's signature Alapin trap in the 4…d6 sub-line. After Bc4 Nb6 e6 Nxc4 Qa4+, Black has to interpose against the queen check. The natural move …Nc6 LOSES because exf7+! drags the king out, then Qxc4+ recovers the bishop and Black's king is permanently exposed on f7/g8. 62 opponents fell into this in his archive, including HansOnTwitch (3161), ckgchess (2888), and pheonixking2000 (2936). The trap line shown is taken directly from his game vs HansOnTwitch (chess.com/game/live/112143011955). Drill the punish so you can find exf7+ over the board the moment Black plays …Nc6.

trapLines.name: d5-Open cxd4 → Nb5 Outpost (17 games incl. Sam Shankland 2934)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 e6 Na3 Nc6 Be3 cxd4 Nb5 Qd8 Nbxd4 Nd5 Nxc6 bxc6
trapLines.explanation: In the d5-Open after Na3 Nc6 Be3, Black's natural …cxd4 (releasing central tension) gets punished by Nb5! — the knight jumps from a3 to b5 attacking the queen on d5 AND the prize square c7. Black has limited queen retreats; …Qd8 (the actual game move in 17 of his wins) loses tempi, then Nbxd4 + Nxc6 trade-down leaves White with structural advantage. The trap line is taken from his game vs remi04 (2836) at chess.com/game/live/77203313889 — the same pattern hit 17 opponents in his data, including Sam Shankland (2934). Drill the Nb5 jump as the punish.

trapLines.name: Bxf7+ → e6+ → Kg8 Walk-In (10 games incl. ShadowKing71 3122)
trapLines.pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+ Bd7 Bc4 Nb6 Bxf7+ Kxf7 e6+ Kg8 exd7 Qxd7 O-O e5 d4 cxd4
trapLines.explanation: In the Bb5+ Bd7 Bc4 Nb6 sub-line of the Nf6 spine, after Bxf7+! Kxf7 e6+, Black has a fork in the road: retreat …Kg8 (gives up castling forever, 10 games) or come forward. The trap line shown takes the …Kg8 retreat — White plays exd7 Qxd7 O-O and Black has lost castling rights, the f7-pawn, the bishop pair... all for one White bishop. From the actual game vs ShadowKing71 (3122) at chess.com/game/live/106030753121. 10 opponents fell into this exact retreat including AlexTruskavetsky (2676) and NovakCabarkapa (2847). When you reach the Bxf7+ check, drill the exd7 follow-up so you can execute it cleanly.

trapLines.name: ...Bg4 Pin Reflex in Nc6 line (7 games)
